title: Tray Design — NP300
description:
TRAY DESIGN — NP300

Kyle from KT Kustoms invited me out to 3D scan this ute chassis for a client tray build he was designing and fabricating.

Using the scan, along with Kyle’s guidance and measurements, I was able to create a visual concept of what he was planning to build for the customer. This was a really fun project, both from the 3D scanning side and the design side.

The scan was done with my old Creality Ferret. It definitely was not designed for large scans like this, and my laptop at the time struggled with the amount of point cloud data, but with time and persistence we managed to get a usable scan. I’m happy with how it came out, and with my new Einstar 2 scanner, large-scale scans like this should be much simpler and higher quality moving forward.

The tray was designed around an APB canopy, APB under-tray boxes, and a Dunn & Watson slide-out trundle drawer. The rear end uses HIMOD Drakon tail lights for a modern finish.

Kyle did an exceptional job bringing this tray to life. Finished product posted over at @ktkustoms25

title: YZF-R7 Pod filter Airbox
description:
YZF-R7 Pod filter Airbox

Scanned. Designed. Printed. Fitted.

This custom R7 airbox started with a full 3D scan of the intake area to capture every mounting point and clearance. I then created a replica model of the DNA pod filter so the fit would be spot on from the start.

The entire airbox was designed in Fusion 360 around the scan data to dial in structure, and fitment.

Printed in multiple materials for the right balance of strength and flexibility:
• ASA-CF for a rigid, heat-resistant, high-strength airbox shell
• TPU for the flexible joiners that clamp securely to the filter and intake

Finished with brass inserts, a serviceable lid, and a hex rear vent for airflow. Clean on the bike. Functional by design.

title: CBR600RR Engine Case Cover
description:
CBR600RR Engine Case Cover

The engine case covers were designed using a 3D scan of the OEM engine case as a dimensional reference, ensuring accurate clearances and perfect fitment before fabrication.

The cover was designed using surface modelling techniques rather than traditional solid modelling; this method produced complex geometry faster and cut model production time in half. (compared to similar previous projects)

The final product is a 4 mm thick wall, solid-infill Engine cover, 3D printed in Carbon Fibre-reinforced nylon; chosen for its strength, heat resistance, low friction, and abrasion resistance — ideal for sacrificial protection in high-impact areas.

title: CBR600RR GP style Front fender Prototype
description:
CBR600RR GP style Front fender Prototype

This design draws heavily from Moto2 aero, especially the Kalex front fender profile. Compared to the OEM hugger, this GP style reduces frontal drag and shields the fork tubes more effectively.

It also pushed me to learn Fusion 360’s surface modeling tools—something I’d barely touched before this. Complex curves like these are where surface techniques really shine.

title: 1780 × 2000 mm Tray — LN106 Single Cab (Beta Design)
description:
1780 × 2000 mm Tray — LN106 Single Cab (Beta Design)

I designed this custom tray for a single-cab LN106.

The tray is built to accommodate APB canopy and under-tray boxes, with integrated mounts for JB74 tail lights and Stedi C4 reverse/flood lights recessed into the rear for a clean, functional look.

The CAD model includes animated moving components, such as opening canopy doors and modular mounting points for accessories, allowing for motion testing and visualizing functionality.

This design is currently in the early development stage, with further refinement planned for structure and detailing. I also have plans to 3D scan the rear cab and chassis to precisely incorporate chassis mounting points and show how the tray will fit and function in a full vehicle setup.

title: Engine covers - cbr600 f2/f3 🏍
description:
Engine covers - cbr600 f2/f3 🏍

I was asked to design and produce a set of engine covers for a rider competing in the Pre-Modern motorcycle racing class.

Replacement covers for earlier model bikes like the CBR600 F2/F3 are extremely hard to find, so I set out to create a Custom, functional alternative.

Using my Creality 3D scanner, I first captured accurate scans of the original engine cases. These were then imported into Fusion 360, where I modelled and refined the covers. It took multiple iterations and fitment test prints to achieve the final design.

The finished parts are printed in PA-CF — a carbon fibre-infused nylon chosen for its high strength, heat resistance, and low friction properties. This material makes the covers highly abrasion-resistant and perfectly suited to the demanding environment near the engine.

title: Subwoofer box - FG falcon Ute
description:
Subwoofer box - FG falcon Ute

One of my first projects after buying my 3D scanner was designing a custom subwoofer enclosure for my 2013 FG Ute.

While off-the-shelf sub boxes exist, finding one that fits perfectly behind the seats is nearly impossible due to the limited space.

Using my Creality 3D scanner, I captured a full-width scan of the rear cabin to model the area accurately. After researching the volume and spacing requirements for proper subwoofer performance, I developed two enclosure designs — a dual 10” and a dual 8” setup.

I’m really happy with how both turned out, and especially with how well I managed to get the 3D scanner dialed in for such a complex space.

title: Axle Sliders
description:
Axle Sliders
These sliders are 3D printed from carbon fibre–infused nylon.

Why nylon? It has a low coefficient of friction and a high melting point, meaning it slides rather than grips on contact — ideal for minimizing damage during an impact. Its slight flexibility also helps absorb shocks, making it perfect for impact-prone parts like axle sliders.

The carbon fibre reinforcement increases stiffness and binds the nylon’s layers, helping prevent splitting or cracking under heavy stress.

⚠️ Downside: CF-nylon is expensive — around 5–6× the cost of standard filament — but the performance and durability make it worth it for functional applications.

Handlebar Quad Lock Mount:
I designed this mount to hold Quad Lock’s charger securely on the handlebars. It’s a two-piece design that slides together and clamps with a bolt and nyloc nut for consistent pressure.

If I were to revisit this design today, I’d:

Integrate a TPU layer (rubber-like material) to improve grip on the metal handlebar.

Add nutserts for easier installation and a cleaner, more refined finish.

Even so, this mount has held up flawlessly for over 12 months, proving the design’s reliability.

title: ’97 Hilux Extra Cab (RN110R) – Tray Build
description:
’97 Hilux Extra Cab (RN110R) – Tray Build

This was the first tray I ever designed and built — completed in November 2023. I created it using a combination of measurements and reference photos to achieve the right proportions and fitment.

It was my first real dive into welding and fabrication, and the project came with plenty of challenges — but also a ton of learning. From material selection to structural rigidity, every step taught me something new about building functional components from scratch.

Looking back now, there are many things I’d do differently. If I were to design another tray today, I’d start by using 3D scanning to eliminate guesswork during the design and fitment stages. This would streamline the process and allow me to have everything precisely mapped out digitally before even purchasing materials.

I’d also incorporate CNC-cut pieces, not only to speed up fabrication but to improve accuracy and repeatability — making it easier to reproduce identical parts or adjust the design for different vehicles. Cutting and shaping the metal manually was by far the most time-consuming (and least consistent) part of the original build.

Overall, this project marked a turning point — where I combined my interest in design, engineering, and fabrication into something tangible.

title: N50 Hilux TOYOTA grill badge
description:
N50 Hilux TOYOTA grill badge 

This was my first 3D print project when I started exploring custom car parts three years ago.

At the time, I didn’t even own a printer — I had the badge printed by a guy I found on Marketplace. But not long after, I bought my first machine: a Bambu P1P.

Two years later, in mid-2025, I revisited the project (even though I’d already sold the car it was originally made for). I completely redesigned the badge from scratch into a cleaner, more functional three-piece setup: adapter, base, and lettering.

The parts are assembled with nutserts, screws, and glue, eliminating the need for supports and cutting production time. I also replaced the hand-painted lettering with solid white plastic, making it more durable — no more fading or scratches.

Proud of how far this project (and my skills) have come since
